segments.text: - Hello, everyone.
Welcome back to Altium Academy.
I'm your host, Zach Peterson,
and today we're gonna be talking
about drill drawings and drill tables.
Now, we got a great question
on one of our Design Review videos,
and we're gonna answer that question

all about drill drawings and
drill tables in this video.
I'll also show you how to create

and configure these
objects in Altium Designer,

so let's go ahead and
jump in and get started.
(upbeat music)

So before we look at
what our drill drawings
and their associated drill tables,
let's take a look at that viewer question.
This question comes

from one of our One Minute
Design Review videos,
and the question comes from Alexander.

He asks, "How do you
create the drill drawing?"
Great question, Alexander.

I'm going to show you
exactly how to do that,
and there are actually two ways to do it,
or there are two acceptable ways

to provide that information
to a manufacturer.
You can do it using a custom drawing

where you export a DXF from
your Altium Designer PCB layout,

or you can create the drawing
inside of Altium Designer.

So I'm gonna show you
how to do it both ways.
But first, for those that aren't familiar,

let's take a look at
what is a drill drawing
and what is a drill table

because you really need
both pieces of information
in order to fabricate a PCB.
So first things first.
I have a PCB open here from Ahmed Aziz,

which was sent in for one of
our One Minute Design Reviews,
and I'm going to show you

what the drill drawing
looks like for this PCB.
Now, in order to create a drill drawing,
there are a few different ways to do it.

I mentioned creating it
from custom drawings,
but you can also export that information
directly as a Gerber file.

So if you go up here to File
and then Fabrication Outputs,

and then you select one
of the Gerber options,
you'll then see a list of layers.
And if you scroll down,

you will see right down here
an entry for drill drawing.

Now if you have an HDI PCB
that has multiple via spans,
you will see multiple options
underneath this drill drawing entry
and you select one of those options
for each of those via spans.

Now here, this is of course
only a two-layer board.
It has through-hole vias,

and so of course we only
have one option here
for top and bottom layer via spans.
So I have that selected.
Now after we select that and we click OK,

and go through the export,
a CAM document opens up,
and then you can see here

we have all of our layers
inside this CAM document.
Now, the default extension
for the drill drawing layer is .gd1.
And so you can see that right here.
And if I just isolate that layer,

you can see right here we
have our drill drawing.

So a drill drawing is a
pretty simple drawing.
You see here we have a bunch of symbols
distributed around the PCB.

If I turn on the solder
mask layer on the top,

you can see where all of these
drill symbols are located.
They're located on all of our vias
and our through-hole pins

as you can see here in this
image in the CAM editor.

In addition to the symbols
that we have in this layout,
we also have a table.

And this table provides
all of the information

needed to understand
each one of the symbols
that's shown in this Gerber layer.

Now you can see here
that the PCB fabricator

is only going to need
four different drills
in order to fully fabricate this PCB.
And the hole sizes or the drill diameters
are listed in this table.

You can also see here we
have a column for plated.
So this would list plated through holes
or non-plated through holes.
In this case,

you can tell these are
all plated through holes.
And then we have a hole type.
So it could be a round hole,
meaning it's just a simple drilled hole,

or you could put slots inside
of a drill table as well.

So a slot could be milled
in with a specific diameter,

and then of course that
mill could extend that slot
for a certain distance.

You could then enter that
information into the drill table.
Here we have the via span,
of course, they're all top to bottom layer

because this is, as I
said, a two-layer PCB,
and then we have a designation

for whether or not this is
a via or a through hole pad.

And then you have some other
information here as well.
You can even have hole tolerances,

which is what I normally
include in these drill tables

because of course that's
generally demanded

by the PCB fabrication
houses that I work with.

So all of this information
was created automatically.

It was generated directly
from the PCB layout.
Now, one thing I want to note
is that if you go into the PCB layout

and you open up the
View Configuration tab,

you'll notice that there is
a layer for a drill drawing.

And if you turn on this
layer and you select it
and then you isolate it,
you actually will find

that you won't see any
of that drill information
except for this drill table.
So this drill information
as far as where the symbols are located,
only gets placed when you export the data
as a fabrication format.
In this case, we did it as Gerber's.
We could also do it as an ODB++ output
or an IPC-2581 output,

and you would be able
to view the same data
in those other formats.
So if you're inside of Altium Designer

and you want to look
at your drill drawing,
don't be surprised
when you turn on your drill drawing layer

and you're not able to see
any of the drill symbols.
Those will get created

when you do your final
export to your Gerber files.
Now that we know what a drill drawing is
and how it can get generated automatically
into your fabrication outputs,
how do we create this drill table?

Well, of course, you
could create it manually,
you could draw out all the lines,
write in all the names for the header.

You could then, you know,
count up all the vias
and create your own symbols.
You can do that yourself.
But of course, inside Altium Designer

there is a tool that will
do this automatically.

So let's go ahead and
jump into another PCB
from one of our viewers.
This one comes from Jefferson Pells,

and it was also sent in for
a One Minute Design Review.

Now we're gonna create the
drill table for this PCB.
In order to do that,

we're gonna turn on the
drill drawing layer,

and then we'll select
the drill drawing layer,
and then we'll go up to Place
and then select the Drill Table option.

And then we just put it wherever
we want inside the layout.
And there we go.
We have our drill table.
Now in this view for this PCB,
I've set this whole thing up

with a drawing outline
and with a title block.
And I've done that

because we're actually creating
the full fabrication drawing
here in this view, in this PCB doc.

So I'll tell you why I wanna
show you that in just a moment.

But for now, take a look
at this drill table.

You see here that when
the drill table comes in,

it comes in with all
the default information.

We may not need to give
all this information
to our fabrication house.

So what we can do is we can
customize this drill table,

and to do that, we go
into the Properties panel,

and then you'll see here
down at the very bottom
we have this option for Edit Columns.
Click on that button
and you'll see here a dialogue comes up
that lets you configure all the columns
that appear in your drill table.

From here, we can add columns,
we can also remove columns.
And in my opinion,

some of these columns should
be removed immediately
because they're really not of any value
to the fabrication house.

Normally, I will remove
the template column.

They don't really need to know
what your drill template is,

they just need to know
what the drill diameter is.

I'll typically remove the
drill layer pair column

because a lot of the
designs that we might do,
they might only be through-hole vias,
so you don't need to include a column
that tells the fabrication house,
that it's all through-hole vias.

You could just put it
into a fabrication note
or you can include a stackup drawing
because the stackup drawing
will also show what the via spans are.

Another one that I may
remove is the via/pad column.
Again, it doesn't really provide
any additional useful information.

And then the pad shape
column I might also remove

because they would be
able to see the shape
just by looking at your copper layers
in the PCB fabrication outputs.

The last item that I might
remove from this table
is the hole type column.
As you can see here in this column,
everything is listed as round
except for a single slot entry here
right at the top of the table.

If you don't have any slots
and they're all round holes,

you can just go ahead
and delete that column

because there's nothing to
differentiate in that column.
And that's it, that's pretty simple.
That's how you place

and edit your drill
drawing in the PCB layout.

Now, what happens if I
place the drill drawing
and then I edit something in the PCB?
First, if I just select this pad,
I go down here to the hole information.
And let's suppose for a moment

that I add a tolerance
plus and minus value.

If I then click away and go
back to my drill drawing,

you'll see here that it's
not showing any tolerances.

Well, if you edit something
in the PCB layout,

what you need to do is go
back here and select this
and click the Refresh button,

and you'll see after I
click that Refresh button,

it then adds in a dedicated
row for that one pad
where I set the hole tolerance values
in the Properties panel.

Once you're satisfied
with your drill table,
you can then go up to the File
and Fabrication Outputs option,
select those drill drawing layers,
and they will export
with the rest of your fabrication outputs.
You can also use an OutJob file.

The OutJob file has entries
for different types of Gerbers
or ODB++ or IPC-2581 exports.

And then you can also select
those drill drawing layers

when you're configuring
those output options
in your OutJob file.
Now, I mentioned earlier

that I was drawing an actual
fabrication drawing here
in this drill drawing layer.
Why would we wanna do that?
Well, one option that you have

for getting this drill drawing
out of your PCB doc file

and into an actual drawing
format is to export a DXF.
Here if you go to File and Export,
you will see an option for DXF or DWG.
You see here that if I click that,

I can go through and do
an export to a DXF file.
If I click that Save button,
you'll see I can then go through here.
I can select my different layers,

I can select component layer
pairs, mechanical layers,
all the important layers.

And you see down here
right near the bottom,
we have an option for a drill drawing.

So I could create a
full fabrication drawing
inside this window in the PCB doc file,

and I can include
whatever fabrication notes
I need to include

and then just export
those mechanical layers
and the drill drawing layers

with all my fabrication
information to an DXF file.

Then I could put it, for
example, into AutoCAD

and do whatever I need to
do to get a final PDF file
to send to my fabrication house.
Now, some companies that I work with
demand that you do this format of drawing
where you basically export a DXF
and then you put it into another template
or put it in with some other drawings,

and then you have a totally
custom drawing format.

But, of course, if you
don't want to do that

or you don't have AutoCAD,
you can use the draftsman tool

inside of Altium Designer to
basically do all the stuff

that we just showed here
in the PCB doc file.
So here I have a fabrication drawing

that I've attached to this
project from Jefferson Pells.

Here you can see that I
have a drill drawing view
shown in this drawing.

Now, in order to place
this drill drawing view,
it's pretty simple,
I just right click, hit Place,

and then here under the
Additional Views option,

you see that we have an
option for a drill drawing

and we can just go ahead and
place that wherever we want.

The other thing I can do is
if I have an existing drawing
in my PCB DWF file
and I bring it into a new project,

I can just right click
and hit Import Changes.
And you see it's gonna take a second,
and then it will automatically update
the existing drill drawing view
with the information in your PCB doc file.
And you can see here that it just updated.

Now, you can also see
here in the draftsman file
that we have a drill table,
and placing a drill table is very simple.
We just right click, go to the Place menu,

and then here you see an
option for Drill Table.
You can just place that wherever you want.

Now, if you select one of
these existing drill tables
and you look in the Properties panel,

you'll see there's also
options to configure
or edit the drill table.
Here, for example, we have an option
where we can edit the drill symbols.
And if I open up the Drill Symbols dialog,

you can see here that I
have some options here
to change the symbol graphic to a letter
or to one of these built-in graphics

that you can see here
in this dropdown menu.
Now, what about editing the columns
in the default drill table?

Well, if you scroll up to the
top of the Properties panel,

you'll see here that
there is a Columns tab,
and here you can show

or hide different columns to
appear in this drill table.
Now, again, here I'm just showing

the need to know information
for the fabrication house.

You can see, of course,
we have the symbol,

we have the corresponding
drill count, the hole size,

plated or non-plated
listed in this column,
and then we have a hole tolerance.

And of course, the hole
tolerance is very important.
That's something

that you have to specify
in the PCB doc file.

Or, if you like, you can
create a fabrication note
and just state in the fabrication note,

for example, all drills
are to have a tolerance
of plus or minus three mil or two mil

or whatever precision
you need for your board.

Now, what should you
do if you have a board
that requires sequential lamination
because it has multiple via spans?
Well, in that case, in my opinion,

you should have a different
drill drawing for each via span.
And the reason is pretty simple.

It's because a lot of
times those via spans
could be on top of each other

in different lamination
regions in the stackup,
and so it can get a little difficult
to see all of those symbols in one spot
in that drill drawing.

If you separate those into
different drill drawings
with their own drill table,

it's much easier to see
all of that information
and it helps you keep things organized
in your fabrication drawing.
Thanks for watching this video, everybody,

and of course, thanks for
leaving those great questions
on all of these YouTube videos.
And if you ask a great question,
it just might end up in its own video,
make sure to hit that Subscribe button,
hit that like button,

leave your comments and questions
in the comments section.
And last, but not least,

don't forget to call
your fabricator folks.
We'll see you next time.
(dramatic music)

title: Creating PCB Drill Drawings and Tables in Altium Designer
